newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss agree to Holocaust memorial fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss agree to Holocaust memorial fund.

text.p: Swiss banks and the government, under pressure from world Jewish groups, agreed on Thursday to create a Holocaust memorial fund as a good will gesture to critics of the neutral country's wartime financial role.

Special ambassador Thomas Borer, the government's top official for the issue, announced the plan after talks with senior executives of Swiss banks, the central bank, insurance companies and other businesses.
Borer told reporters that details remained to be worked out and no amount of money had been fixed for the fund, the idea of which had been resisted by Berne and the banks for months.

"We certainly hope that this (fund) will be understood as a sign of our goodwill," Borer said, referring to demands from the World Jewish Congress and other critics that Switzerland make a gesture of remorse for profiting from World War Two.
"All the major banks support this idea, as well as other companies," Borer said.
"We did not talk about an amount. It would be premature to bring numbers into play," he added.
One of the top Swiss bankers, Credit Suisse Group chairman Rainer Gut, had called on Wednesday for a Holocaust memorial fund much larger than 100 million Swiss francs.

The fund is part of Berne's efforts to calm criticism that the neutral country cynically exploited the war, including claims Swiss banks hoarded accounts left by Holocaust victims and that the central bank bought looted Nazi gold.

Swiss banks last year set up an ombudsman and a joint commission with Jewish groups to find the heirs for Holocaust money. Berne meanwhile has named an international panel of historians to review the broader Swiss wartime financial role.

Borer said his foreign ministry task force, charged with coordinating Switzerland's response to the crisis, would lead efforts to put together details of the fund, including who should put in how much money and its exact purpose.

"Its goals will have something to do with the Holocaust in the widest sense," Borer said, naming projects to fight discrimination and racism as well as support for Holocaust survivors as possible aims.
"These are the kinds of projects that Jewish groups have repeatedly mentioned to us," he said.
Berne had previously insisted any payments would have to wait for proof of Swiss misdeeds from the panel of historians, which could take up to five years to report.

But resistance melted this month after Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz accused the WJC of blackmailing Berne, drawing Jewish ire that nearly flaired into a diplomatic crisis and was defused only after two weeks when Delamuraz apologised.
Borer said it was too early to tell when the fund would be finalised but added it was more a matter of weeks than months.

"The fund can be set up fairly rapidly on financing from private businesses. That would be one way of satisfying the sort of urgency that is present because of the age of Holocaust survivors," he said.

Borer said the government would not commit any money until a historical review expected by mid-year of Switzerland's anti-Jewish wartime refugee policy and its centyral bank gold purchases from Nazi Germany.
"But the government is taking an active part in this humanitarian gesture by taking charge of seeing that this fund is realised," he added.
